title: Milestone: Knowledge, Mind and Morals
objective: After this level you can connect the first half's traditions, theories of knowledge, views of the mind and moral theories into one map of philosophy's big questions.
summary: Ethics offers three main answers (consequences, duty, character), plus care; metaethics asks whether morality is relative, depends on God, or can follow from facts.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to fold the map.
cards.body: You’ve met theories of what is real, how we know and what a self is. This milestone lays out the moral half, the part that asks how to live, as one map.

cards.headline: Three answers to one good deed
cards.body: Someone in need should obviously be helped. But why? A utilitarian points to consequences: helping maximizes well-being. A deontologist points to duty, a moral rule. A virtue ethicist points to character: helping is charitable or kind. These are the three major approaches in normative ethics. Care ethics, set against the rule and consequence approaches, starts from relationships instead.

items.label: Consequences
points: Bentham: pain and pleasure are our masters
Mill: some pleasures are higher in kind

items.label: Duty
points: Kant: could everyone act on your maxim?
Kant: never treat people merely as means

items.label: Character
points: Aristotle: courage is a mean between two vices
Aristotle: virtue is built by practice

cards.headline: The floor underneath
cards.body: Below all of these sits metaethics. It steps back from particular moral debates to ask what morality itself is. Are there moral facts? Are moral standards culturally relative? Does morality depend on God’s commands? Can an ought follow from an is? Here Level 2’s metaphysics, the study of what exists, and epistemology, the study of knowledge, turn to ethics.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway there
learned: How consequences, duty and character give three different reasons to help someone in need.
Why the Euthyphro dilemma and Hume’s is and ought make morality’s foundations hard to pin down.
What Herodotus’s funeral story suggests about relativism, and why critics point to reformers.
Why Mencius thought goodness grows from sprouts while Xunzi thought it must be built.

questions.prompt: Milestone recap: which of these was one of the Nyaya school’s four means of knowledge?

options.label: Dreaming
options.rationale: Not on Nyaya’s list.

options.label: Royal decree
options.rationale: Not on Nyaya’s list; testimony is, but not decree.

options.label: Guesswork
options.rationale: Not on Nyaya’s list.

questions.explanation: Nyaya counted perception, inference, comparison and testimony as the four means of knowledge.

questions.prompt: Milestone recap: where did India’s Carvaka materialists say consciousness comes from?

options.label: From Brahman, the reality under everything
options.rationale: That’s nearer Advaita Vedanta.

options.label: From an eternal soul
options.rationale: The Carvakas denied any such soul.

options.label: From the gods’ commands
options.rationale: The Carvakas trusted perception, not the gods.

questions.explanation: The Carvakas argued that consciousness is a product of the material body: no body, no mind.

questions.prompt: Milestone recap: what lesson did Herodotus draw from Darius’s questions to the Greeks and Callatians?

options.label: Every people thinks its own customs are best
Greek customs are the most rational
options.rationale: He drew the opposite lesson.

options.label: Customs never change
options.rationale: The story isn’t about change.

options.label: Kings should decide which customs are right
options.rationale: Darius only asked; he didn’t rule.

questions.explanation: Herodotus concluded that each people would choose its own customs as the best, and agreed that custom is lord of all.

questions.prompt: Milestone recap: where did Mencius and Xunzi each look for the guide to becoming good?

options.label: Both looked only to the law
options.rationale: Neither rested on law alone.

options.label: Mencius outward to ritual, Xunzi inward to sprouts
options.rationale: That’s reversed.

options.label: Neither thought people could become good
options.rationale: Both thought everyone can become good, with effort.

options.label: Mencius inward to the heart, Xunzi outward to the sages’ rituals

questions.explanation: Both held anyone can become good; Mencius looked inward to the sprouts, Xunzi outward to rituals handed down by the sages.

questions.prompt: A friend helps a stranger in need because doing so is kind and charitable. Which approach explains the act that way?

options.label: Consequentialism
options.rationale: That would point to the best consequences.

options.label: Deontology
options.rationale: That would point to a moral rule.

options.label: Relativism
options.rationale: That’s a view about moral truth, not a reason to help.

questions.explanation: Pointing to the kindness or charity of the act is the virtue ethicist’s answer, focused on character.

questions.prompt: Which of these questions belongs to metaethics rather than normative ethics?

options.label: Should I keep this promise?
options.rationale: That asks what to do, a normative question.

options.label: Is it kind to tell her the truth?
options.rationale: That asks about a particular act.

options.label: Which charity should I give to?
options.rationale: That asks what to do.

questions.explanation: Metaethics steps back to ask what morality itself is, such as whether moral standards are relative to cultures.

questions.prompt: Milestone recap: the ring of Gyges from Level 3 returned in Level 43. What did Glaucon finally ask Socrates to show?

options.label: That justice always brings the best reputation and rewards
options.rationale: Reputation was ruled out.

options.label: That the ring really existed
options.rationale: The ring was a story, not a claim.

options.label: That injustice is better if unseen
options.rationale: That’s the view Glaucon wanted refuted.

options.label: That justice is worth having in itself, seen or unseen

questions.explanation: Glaucon asked Socrates to praise justice only for what it does to its possessor, whether seen or unseen by gods and men.
